text_summary.body: A year after the dream, walking on his palace roof, the king boasted that he had built great Babylon by his own power. A voice from heaven announced that the kingdom had departed from him; he was driven from men, ate grass like oxen and was wet with dew until his hair and nails grew long. At the end of the days his reason returned, he blessed the Most High, and he was restored with greater majesty.

setting.body: Nebuchadnezzar was renowned as a builder at Babylon; most of his roughly fifty known inscriptions concern building, such as the East India House foundation tablet. Nabonidus, the last Neo-Babylonian king, was absent at the Arabian oasis of Tayma for years while "the prince" held Babylonia (Nabonidus Chronicle), and a Qumran text (4Q242) tells of Nabonidus's seven-year affliction at Tayma.

assumptions: As narrated, the episode falls within Nebuchadnezzar's reign (605–562).

competing_reconstructions.label: A historical illness of Nebuchadnezzar
competing_reconstructions.summary: Babylonian royal records would not record a king's incapacity; Guzik cites Abydenus (via Eusebius) on Nebuchadnezzar being "possessed" and a gap in records c. 582–575 BC. Some read the fragmentary text BM 34113 as relating to Nebuchadnezzar's later years (not verified here; the museum catalogues it as concerning Amel-Marduk).

competing_reconstructions.label: A Nabonidus tradition transferred to Nebuchadnezzar
competing_reconstructions.summary: Nabonidus's long absence at Tayma, rumours of his illness, and the Qumran Prayer of Nabonidus (seven years, Tayma, a Judean, acknowledgement of God) suggest the story originally concerned him.

competing_reconstructions.label: A medical condition (boanthropy)
competing_reconstructions.summary: The symptoms resemble a recognised delusional condition in which a person believes himself an animal. This is an interpretive medical analogy, not a diagnosis supported by Babylonian evidence.

commentary.paraphrase: Guzik sees the episode as God humbling the proud king, interprets the "seven times" as seven years, and draws the lesson that understanding returned when the king looked up to heaven.

open_questions: Read Grayson (BHLT) and the BM record for BM 34113.
